Yuki onna may also be known as yuki-musume ("snow daughter"), yuki-onago ("snow girl"), yukijorō (雪女郎, "snow woman"), yuki anesa ("snow sis'"), yuki-onba ("snow granny" or "snow nanny"), yukinba ("snow hag") in Ehime, yukifuri-baba ("snowfall hag") in Nagano. Yuki-onna also has many names that come from the Japanese word for icicle, like tsurara-onna, kanekori-musume and shigama-nyōbō.

Yumjao Leima or Yumjao Lairembi or Yumjao Lairemma is the mother goddess of house, household, royalty, rule and power in Meitei mythology and religion. She is designated as the all time ruling Queen Mother. Legend says she assumes a human form in white clothes and blesses kings. She is one of the divine incarnations of Leimarel Sidabi. In Meitei language (Manipuri language), "Yumjao" means "large house" or "big house". "Yumjao" or "Yimjao" may also refer to "Royal House". In Meitei language (Manipuri language), "Leima" means "Queen". In Meitei language (Manipuri language), "Lairembi" means "goddess". The Meitei language (Manipuri language) word "Lairemma" is also another term for "goddess". Meitei King Naothingkhong (c. 7th century) of Ancient Kangleipak (Antique Manipur) built a temple dedicated to goddess Yumjao Lairembi. Goddess Yumjao Leima appears in a human form in white clothes to come to bless her son, the King of the kingdom. Even during the death of a king, she came to the place in the form of a mortal being. She controls the life and the death of the kings. She is the chief of the household and the guidance of the kings. According to beliefs, Goddess Yumjao Leima is the divine representation of the Queen Mother (Royal Mother) of the kingdom. All the powerful queen mothers were integrated into goddess Yumjao Leima after their death. Goddess Yumjao Leima herself was the all-time ruling Queen Mother. The most powerful person in a kingdom was always the Queen Mother - representation of Goddess Yumjao Leima. In ancient Kangleipak, cut off heads of the enemies from the war were offered to the goddess. The Meitei kings ruled the kingdom in the name of their Queen Mothers. Battles and wars were conducted in the name of the Queen Mothers. One example is that of an event recorded in the Cheitharol Kumbaba: Goddess Yumjao Leima is prayed for the longevity of life of the King. The final rites and rituals dedicated to Her are generally performed by the maibas. Goddess Yumjao Lairemma is mainly worshipped by the Thaopicham family of Meitei ethnicity. According to Meitei culture, the "Nongmai" class is in the middle position of the society of the maibis (priestesses). They used to take care of the cult of goddess Yumjao Lairembi. The "Temple of Yumjao Lairembi" inside the Kangla is at the left side of the Temple of Pakhangba. Structurally, both the temples are of the same architectural styles. The southern wall of the temple is well decorated. The remaining three walls of the temple are of little decorations. A door with the lancite arch is in the southern wall of the temple. Two false doors surround the two sides of the one real door. All the doors (real and false) are framed with pilasters. The ground plan of the temple is in square shape. Its area covered is 2.43 square meters. In October 2011, a temple named "Ima Ibemma Yumjao Lairembi Shanglen" was built in honor of goddess Yumjao Lairembi in Thangmeiband town in Imphal. A temple dedicated to Yumjao Lairembi of Arambam region is in Imphal West district in Manipur. "Yumjao Lairembi Temple" is in Meino Leirak, Sagolband, Imphal, Manipur. "Thaoroijam Yumjao Lairembi Temple" is in Thaoroijam Mamang Leikai, Nambol, Manipur. The "Yumjao Lairembi Dramatic and Cultural Union" is a nonprofit dramatic union. It was established in Khagempali Huidrom Leikai, Imphal in the year 2011.

Yves Saint Laurent SAS (,,, ), also known as Saint Laurent and YSL, is a French luxury fashion house founded in 1961 by Yves Saint Laurent and his partner, Pierre Bergé. The company focuses on ready-to-wear, leather accessories, and footwear. Its cosmetics line, YSL Beauty, is owned by L'Oréal. A total of 282 boutiques are in operation across 48 countries, as of May 2026:

Yōkai, also known as ghost-and-monsters or god-and-demons or simply ghost-monsters or god-demons, are undead creatures in old Japanese stories, such as oni, kappa or tengu. They have mysterious supernatural powers. There are thousands of yōkai. In the Edo period, yōkai were characters in story books. Recently, many new yōkai have been made. There is even a yōkai dictionary. The yōkai are ghost/monster or deity/demon hybrids in Japanese tradition. In the past people believed they caused disease, accidents and natural disasters. People were often scared of them. The most famous yōkai are Tengu, Oni (Japanese ogre), and Kyubi no Kitsune (a fox with nine tails). When some people and animals are filled with hate, they became yōkai. For example, Sutoku. Sutoku (Japanese ancient emperor) died filled with hate. Then, he became a Tengu and caused a disaster. Also, a cat which lived too long time became Nekomata. Recently, yōkai are familiar with people as subculture in Japan. In recent decades, the yōkai have been frequently depicted in Japanese fiction and media, particularly in horror or fantasy-themed works, such as in manga, anime and films, as well as in videogames, a notable example of this is the manga GeGeGe no Kitarō, written by mangaka Shigeru Mizuki, of which is entirely based on the yōkai myth. Other examples includes the manga series Death Note, Pet Shop of Horrors, Good Luck Girl!, light novel Ghost Hunt, the 2011 animated film A Letter to Momo and RPG videogame franchise Yo-kai Watch.

The Zabur is what the Qur'an describes God revealing to David. It contains psalms, which are poetic prayers of praise and worship. The Qur'an says: "We sent inspiration to Abraham, Isma'il, Isaac, Jacob and the Tribes, to Jesus, Job, Jonah, Aaron, and Solomon, and to David We gave the Psalms" (Qur'an 4:163).

Zakat is one of the five most important aspects of Islam. Zakat means giving charity to the poor. Generally, a Muslim is expected to give zakat as long as they are able. Through Zakat wealth reaches to the poor class of the society. It is considered to be a personal responsibility for Muslims to help those in need and eliminate inequality. It is often 2.5% of what the Muslim has.

The Zaidiyyah are a Shia Muslim sect are different from the usual Shia Islam because of the argument over the who is the fifth Imam, or religious leader. They believe the fifth Imam was Zaid ibn Ali, but most other Shia Muslims believe that it was his brother, Muhammad. Zaydi Muslims also follow a long list of other imams after Zayd Bin Ali and believe that the Imam is not appointed by God, unlike other Shia Muslims. Zaydis are different from other Shia Muslims also by prohibiting mut'ah (temporary marriage), not performing taqlid (conforming to the opinion and understanding of a teacher), and believing imams can make mistakes and then should be overthrown. Today, they make up 40% of the population of Yemen, including the country's president. There are also Zaidis in Najran, Saudi Arabia. Jarudiyya is a Zaydi sect that curses Abu Bakr and the rest of the companions for not giving the caliphate to Ali. It believes like Twelvers that Ali was the rightful caliph. Jarudiyya sect has special admiration for Amina, the Mother of the Prophet. Sulaymaniyya is a Zaydi sect that believes that the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar were mistakes and that Ali was the rightful caliph. Its beliefs are rooted in both Twelvers and Sunnis. Salihiyya is a Zaydi sect that believes, similarly to Sulaymaniyya, that the caliphates of Abu Bakr and Umar were mistakes but also accepts the caliphates of the other companions of Muhammad. It has the closest beliefs to those of Sunnis.

Zahurul Islam Khan Bikalpa Dhara Bangladesh politician. He was elected a member of parliament from Mymensingh-9 in February 1996. Khan was elected to parliament from Mymensingh-9 as a Bangladesh Nationalist Party candidate in 15 February 1996 Bangladeshi general election. He joined the Jatiya Party and was defeated by Mymensingh-9 seat in the seventh election on 12 June 1996. He joined the Bikalpa Dhara Bangladesh party in 2004 and lost the Mymensingh-9 seat in the 2008 ninth national election. He then joined the Awami League.
Zahhak or Azhi Dahāka is an evil character in Iranian (Persian) mythology and folklore. He appears in the texts of the Avesta in the Zoroastrian religion.

Zahran Alloush was a leader of Jaysh al-Islam and was a big part of the Islamic Front where he was a military chief and was called one of the powerful people in Syria. He was born in Douma in 1971 and was married to 3 wives. He was killed by a Syrian-Russian airstrike on the 25th of December 2015 and was succeeded by Essam al-Buwaydhani as leader of Jaysh al-Islam.

The Zamzam Well (, Biʾr Zamzam) is a historic well located within the Masjid al-Haram in Mecca, Saudi Arabia, approximately 20 metres (66 ft) east of the Kaaba, the holiest site in Islam. The well is about 30 metres (98 ft) deep and is topped by a dome in an underground chamber. Millions of pilgrims visit the well annually during Hajj and Umrah to drink its water, which is distributed through fountains in the mosque and bottled for takeaway. In Islamic tradition, the well is considered a miraculous source of water provided by God. It is believed to have originated thousands of years ago to save Hagar (Hājar) and her infant son Ishmael (Ismāʿīl) from thirst in the desert. The water is regarded as blessed, and hadiths attribute healing and spiritual properties to it when consumed with sincere intention. Geologically, the well taps into a fractured rock aquifer recharged by rainfall in the surrounding valleys. It has been managed and studied extensively in modern times by Saudi authorities to ensure sustainability and safety. According to Islamic tradition, the Zamzam Well originated during the time of the prophet Abraham (Ibrāhīm). On divine command, Abraham left his wife Hagar and their son Ishmael in the barren valley of Mecca (then known as Bakkah). When their provisions ran out, Hagar desperately searched for water, running seven times between the hills of Safa and Marwa. In distress, the infant Ishmael scraped the ground with his foot (or, in some narrations, the angel Gabriel (Jibrīl) struck the earth), causing water to gush forth. Hagar contained the flow by building a barrier, exclaiming "Zamzam" (meaning "stop" or "abound" in ancient Arabic), which gave the well its name. This spring attracted the tribe of Jurhum, who settled in the area with Hagar's permission. Over centuries, the well remained a vital source but was eventually buried or lost, possibly due to siltation, conflict, or deliberate concealment by the Jurhum tribe before their expulsion from Mecca. The well was rediscovered in the late 6th century CE by Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim, grandfather of the Prophet Muhammad. Guided by dreams, Abd al-Muttalib excavated the site, uncovering ancient artifacts (including gazelles and swords from the Kaaba) and restoring the water flow. Disputes arose with the Quraysh tribe over ownership, but Abd al-Muttalib retained control. The responsibility for providing Zamzam water to pilgrims (siqāya) passed through his family, including his son al-Abbas. Throughout Islamic history, the well has been cleaned, reinforced, and expanded multiple times: During the Abbasid era (e.g., under Caliph al-Amin in the 8th–9th century CE), reinforcements were added. In pre-modern times, it featured structures for drawing water with buckets and pulleys. In the 20th century, under Saudi rule, pumps were installed (starting in the 1950s–1960s), and the well was enclosed in a basement chamber during expansions of the Masjid al-Haram. Major cleanings occurred in 1379 AH (1959–1960 CE) and 1399 AH (1979 CE), increasing flow rates. In 931 CE, during the Qarmatian raid on Mecca, the well was reportedly damaged or filled with corpses, but it was later restored. Zamzam holds profound spiritual importance in Islam. Drinking its water is a recommended act during Hajj and Umrah. The Prophet Muhammad is reported to have said: "The water of Zamzam is for whatever it is drunk for" (narrated in Sunan Ibn Majah and others), implying blessings based on the drinker's intention (e.g., for healing, knowledge, or forgiveness). The ritual of Sa'i (walking between Safa and Marwa) commemorates Hagar's search. Pilgrims often drink Zamzam while facing the Kaaba, making supplications. The well is hand-excavated, approximately 30 metres deep, with a diameter of 1.08–2.66 metres. It draws from a renewable aquifer fed by rainfall infiltration from Wadi Ibrahim and surrounding hills, flowing through fractured granite and bedrock. Pumping rates are regulated (11–18.5 litres per second) to prevent depletion. The Saudi Geological Survey operates the Zamzam Studies and Research Centre (established in the late 20th century), which monitors water levels, quality, and recharge using digital systems. Daily testing ensures safety, and extraction is limited during high-demand periods like Hajj and Ramadan. Despite high usage (supplying millions annually), the well has never dried up, attributed to sustainable management and natural recharge. Zamzam is alkaline mineral water, classified as sodium-calcium-bicarbonate type. It is rich in calcium (around 93–200 mg/L), magnesium (38–42 mg/L), sodium (133–250 mg/L), and fluoride (0.7–0.74 mg/L), with higher total dissolved solids (TDS) than typical drinking water (around 600–900 mg/L, exceeding some aesthetic guidelines but within WHO limits for safety). Microbiologically, it remains free of bacteria and algae due to natural fluoride and flow dynamics. Trace elements like arsenic, lead, and cadmium are below WHO permissible limits in official tests. Some older reports (e.g., a 2011 BBC investigation on exported samples) alleged elevated arsenic or nitrates, but Saudi authorities and subsequent studies attribute discrepancies to contamination during handling or fake products, affirming source water safety. Studies confirm no toxicity, with potential benefits like hypolipidemic and uricosuric effects in animal models, though comparable to other mineral waters. Today, the well's opening is sealed, and water is pumped to fountains, coolers, and a bottling facility (King Abdullah Zamzam Water Project, inaugurated 2010, costing SAR 700 million). Bottled Zamzam is distributed free to pilgrims but cannot be commercially sold outside Saudi Arabia. Saudi Geological Survey – Zamzam Studies and Research Centre reports. Al-Azraqi, Akhbar Makkah (historical accounts). Ibn Hisham, Sirat Rasul Allah (biography of Muhammad). Various hydrochemical studies (e.g., Khalid et al., 2014; Shomar, 2012).

Zayd ibn Harithah (, DIN) (c. 581–629 CE), was a Companion of the Prophet of Islam and his adopted son. He is the only Companion whose name appears in the Qur'an. * indicates that the marriage order is disputed Note that direct lineage is marked in bold.

Zechariah was the father of John the Baptist. He appears in the Gospel of Luke and the Quran. He was struck dumb by an angel for failing to have faith. His voice was restored after John was born.Zecheriah is considered a prophet in Islam

Zelus (, zeal) is the god of dedication and emulation in Greek mythology. He is the son of Styx and Pallas, and also the brother of Nike, Cratos, and Bia. He and his brothers and sister were the friends of Zeus and were always with him. He was a constant companion of Zeus and personified zeal.

Zionism is a nationalist movement that advocates for the creation and support of a homeland for the Jewish people in the Land of Israel. Amongst Jews living in Israel, Zionism is generally associated with a conservative religious worldview. The modern movement started in the late 19th century in Europe, as a reaction to increasing antisemitism and to ideas of assimilation. Zionism has had many different varieties that all shared the goal of creating a homeland for the Jewish People. The dominant variety at first was political Zionism, led by Theodor Herzl, but it later lost ground to the socialist Labor Zionism. In 1948, Zionism resulted in the creation of the State of Israel in a portion of the Jewish ancestral homeland. The word "Zionism" was first used in 1890. It comes from Zion, meaning Jerusalem, though it can also symbolically mean the Land of Israel as a whole. Jewish people at the time lived as minority groups among other nations all across the world, in what was called the diaspora. In the early 19th century, assimilation and legal emancipation were popular ideas among Jews in western Europe. However, in the late 19th century anti-Semitism became a bigger threat, with the 1881 Russian pogroms and the Dreyfus affair in France. This caused some Jewish thinkers to lose faith in the idea of ever being accepted in gentile societies. One of these thinkers was Theodor Herzl, who is often considered the father of modern Political Zionism. In his book, the Jewish State, Herzl writes that the distinct status of Jews neither can, nor should, be changed. Instead he believed that antisemitism could be stopped by making the Jewish people a nation like any other, through giving them their own land. At the time there were multiple territories up for consideration, the most important being Argentina and Palestine. Herzl argues in favor of Palestine, thinking it would attract more people because of its status as the historic homeland of the Jews. Political Zionism was a secular movement and it was out of pragmatic considerations, rather than religious beliefs, that Palestine was chosen. In 1897 Herzl led the First Zionist Congress. There the Basel Program was adopted, espousing political Zionism and a Jewish homeland in the Land of Israel. The World Zionist Organization was created at the congress to support this goal. There were many more congresses after this, and at the fifth Zionist Congress in 1901 the Jewish National Fund was established with the goal of purchasing land in Palestine. Political Zionism wanted to work with the established powers to get a publicly recognized and legally assured homeland. Palestine at the time was under the control of the Ottoman Empire, but Herzl's attempts to get support from the Ottomans failed, and he had to appeal to the imperial powers of Europe. Herzl negotiated with British and Russian officials to use their influence to get official support for a Jewish homeland in Palestine, but this failed as well. In 1903 the British offered Herzl a Jewish homeland in Uganda instead, but this was eventually rejected by the Zionist congress. Only during World War I did the Zionist movement get the great power support they had been seeking. In 1917 the British signed the Balfour Declaration, wherein they declared that they "favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people". Part of the British motivation in signing was getting support of Jews in Russia and the U.S.A. for the allied cause. After the war, the British Empire took control of Palestine and administered it as their own colony, the Mandate of Palestine. During this time the cooperation between the Zionist movement and the British continued, though there were still tensions. The alliance would fall apart just before World War II. Organized Jewish migration into Palestine began after the pogroms of 1881 with the Hibbat Zion movement. However, even when they later joined forces with the Zionist congress it remained a small movement, as most Jewish migrants went to the United States. Only 3% of the Jews fleeing eastern Europe between 1881 and World War I went to Palestine. In the first wave of migration, known as the first Aliyah, the Jewish immigrants established agricultural colonies called moshavot. These settlements were poor, and so the immigrants turned to outside sponsors for help, who funded the development of other systems. The farms were turned into wine and citrus plantations based on the model of French Algeria, where they employed mostly cheaper Palestinian labor. Jewish workers had to compete with Palestinian workers, which lowered their wages. The immigrants of the second Aliyah of 1905 included many socialists. They thought that they needed higher wages for the Jewish workers in order to attract immigrants for the Zionist project. They wanted a "conquest of labor", fighting the landowners for better working conditions, but also trying to exclude Arab workers from these jobs to give them to Jewish workers. This was the beginning of Labor Zionism, which would overtake Political Zionism as the dominant variety after World War I. Labor Zionism was influenced by socialist ideals, and believed that to build a Jewish state a strong Jewish working class had to be created as well. They established farms called kibbutzim where all the workers collectively owned the land. In 1920 they formed the Histadrut, a trade union that eventually gained control of large sectors of the economy, becoming one of the largest employers for Jewish workers. The secretary of the Histadrut, David Ben-Gurion, became the unofficial leader of the Zionist movement in 1935 when he became chairman of the Jewish Agency. In 1948 he declared the establishment of a Jewish State in the Land of Israel and became Israel's first prime minister. Some Zionists believe that Israel should control the West Bank and the Gaza Strip. Other Zionists support a Two-state solution in which Israel and Palestine are separate countries. The entire region is the subject of the Israeli–Palestinian conflict. Out of the conflict and segregation in Palestine, African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights of African Union condemns Zionism as human rights violation, as well as apartheid and colonialism.

Zion is one of the seventy names of Jerusalem, and in the Bible is the second name for Jerusalem after the name "Jerusalem". The name "Zion" originally revolves around a certain area in the city. It is customary to delineate the site in the eastern and southern part of Jerusalem during the Second Temple period, including the City of David, the Ophel and Mount Moriah.

Zionism as settler colonialism is an idea. It says that the movement to create a Jewish state in Palestine is a kind of colonization that pushed out the people who already lived there. This idea is mainly used by people who criticize Zionism and Israel. Early Zionist leaders, like Theodor Herzl and Ze’ev Jabotinsky, sometimes used words like “colonize,” but the formal idea of settler colonialism didn’t exist until the 1960s. Later, scholars like Edward Said and Maxime Rodinson applied this idea to Zionism. This way of thinking became more popular during the 1960s, when many countries were gaining independence from colonizers. In the 1990s, some Israeli and Palestinian historians called the Nakba (the 1948 Palestinian displacement) an ongoing process, saying Zionism tries to remove or absorb Palestinians, similar to what happened to Native Americans in the U.S. or Aboriginal people in Australia. People who disagree with this idea, like Benny Morris, say that Zionism is about Jewish people returning to their historic homeland and having the right to govern themselves. The argument is really about history, identity, and who has the right to the land. Many early Zionist leaders openly described their movement as a form of colonization. Vladimir Jabotinsky called Zionism “a colonization adventure,” while Theodor Herzl referred to it as “something colonial” and spoke of “experiments in colonization” in Palestine. Max Nordau also described Zionism as a large-scale colonization effort, rejecting smaller, gradual settlement. Major Zionist institutions reflected this identity, with names such as the Jewish Colonization Association, the Palestine Jewish Colonization Association, and the Jewish Colonial Trust. Early Zionist groups promoted “Hebrew labor,” encouraging Jewish-owned businesses to hire only Jews and acquire land that could never be sold to non-Jews. Collective farms, or kibbutzim, were created to build self-sufficient Jewish communities and later served as models for settlements beyond Israel’s 1967 borders. Chaim Weizmann compared the Zionist project to French colonization in Tunisia, saying he hoped Jewish immigration would make Palestine “as Jewish as England is English.” Anthropologist Scott Atran noted, however, that unlike the French, Zionist colonization sought to replace Arab labor, not rely on it. In 1948, about 750,000 Palestinians fled or were expelled during the Nakba, and around 500 villages were destroyed. While some Israelis saw this as a tragic consequence of war, some historians describe it as ethnic cleansing. Palestinian lands were seized, and those who remained in Israel were confined to restricted areas. In 1956, Israeli military leader Moshe Dayan acknowledged this reality, saying: “We are a generation of settlers… without the steel helmet and cannon we cannot plant a tree and build a home.” Historian Arnon Degani argues that the end of military rule over Palestinian citizens in 1966 marked a shift from colonial to settler-colonial governance. After the 1967 war, Israel captured the Golan Heights and the West Bank, displacing large portions of their Syrian and Palestinian populations. The “settler colonial framework” for analyzing the Palestinian struggle initially emerged in the 1960s, as decolonization was happening across Africa and the Middle East. This perspective was revived in the 1990s within Israeli academic circles, particularly by Israeli and Palestinian “New Historians.” These scholars challenged Israel’s foundational myths and considered the “Nakba” (the 1948 displacement of Palestinians) an ongoing process. This resurgence coincided with a shift in focus from supporting a “two-state solution” to advocating for a “one-state solution” that mandates equal citizenship for all, thereby challenging the Jewish identity of Israel. According to The Economist, the Palestinian diaspora has redefined the Israeli-Palestinian conflict — shifting it from “a clash between two national movements” to “a generational struggle for liberation against settler colonialism.” This view has gained strong support among left-leaning university activists.
Zlín Region is an administrative unit (kraj) of the Czech Republic. The capital city is Zlín. The Zlín Region is divided into 4 districts: Holešov with its museum of Jewish culture

Zohurul Hoque (Bengali: জহুুুুুুুুুুুুরুুল হক; Assamese: জহৰুুুুুুুুুুুুুুুুল হক; October 11, 1926 - January 18, 2017), was an Indian Muslim figure from Assam who is the only figure noted for the translation of the Quran in three languages, which were Bengali, Assamese and English. Along with the translation by Muhiuddin Khan, his Bengali translation of the Quran is one of the most used, but it is not famous in terms of built-up structure of the translation of the certain verses in the Quran, unlike Muhiuddin Khan who did.

The Zomi Baptist Church is a christian believer church. In India the Zomi Baptist Church (ZBC) was established in 1982. The ZBC headquarters is at Champhai, India. In Myanmar the ZBC is known as ZBCM (Zomi Baptist Church in Myanmar). Nowadays the ZBC is also present in the United States (Tulsa) and other countries in the world.

Zurvan is the creator god in, a form of Zoroastrianism. He is a personification of time and eternity. He is the father of Ahura Mazda and his enemy Angra Mainyu. His name comes from the Middle Persian term zurwān ("Time"), which derives from the Avestan zruvā ("Time"). Words carved in stone that include the letters zrw(n) and zraovo were discovered. These words make people think that in Sogdiana and Bactria, Zurvan was worshipped like a main god. In the third century, his name was used by the Manichaeans, for the father of greatness

`Abdu'l-Bahá was a Persian man who was born on 23 May 1844 and died on 28 November 1921. His father was Bahá'u'lláh who founded the religion known as the Bahá'í Faith. `Abdu'l-Bahá spent most of his adult life in prison or under arrest, because of his father's new religion. Bahá'u'lláh called him the "Expounder" of his word, meaning that only `Abdu'l-Bahá had the right to say what Bahá'u'lláh's writings mean. This was to prevent different people from splitting the religion up because they thought Bahá'u'lláh meant different things, the way many other religions have split up.

Áedán mac Gabráin or Áedan of Dalriada was the first king of Scotland that historians know lived in real life. He was not only a legend or myth. Stories say he was the son of King Gabhran mac Domangairt. Aedan's son, Eochaid Buide, became king after him in the early sixth century. He ascended the throne in the 570s. One source says Aedan died in 608.

The Cathedral of Ávila is a Romanesque and Gothic church. It is in Ávila. It is just south of Old Castile, Spain. It also has a cemetery. It was built in 1475. The Cathedral of Ávila was one of 100 finalists for the 12 Treasures of Spain in 2007.
Ásynja (plural: asynjur) refers to Norse mythology. Female gods in Norse mythology are called Ásynja. The male gods are called Æsir; there are 14 Æsir, and there are also 14 asynjur.

Anu is the Mesopotamian god of the sky. The Sumerians describe him as the embodiment of the sky which can come to Earth in human form. Anu is also the King of Gods, and sometimes said to create humans with the assistance of his sons Enlil and/or Enki Anu is not talked about in the Hebrew scriptures.

The Æsir (Old Norse: singular ǫ́ss or áss; feminine ásynja, plural ásynjur) are the main group or tribe of deities in Norse mythology. Including Odin, Frigg, Thor, and Baldr, the Æsir reside in the realm of Asgard, at the top of Yggdrasil's highest branch. Alongside the Æsir is a second family of gods, known as the Vanir, who joined with the Æsir to form a single, unified pantheon after the devastating war between the two tribes of deities. The Vanir were native to Vanaheimr, the god Njörðr and his children, Freyr and Freyja chief among them. The Æsir gods were usually connected with power and war, and the Vanir were associated with fertility and nature. The things that happened between the Æsir and the Vanir are an interesting part of Norse mythology. While other cultures have had "elder" and "younger" generations of gods, as with the Titans and the Olympians of ancient Greece, the Æsir and Vanir were portrayed as contemporaries. The two tribes fought battles, concluded treaties, and exchanged hostages. Freyr and Freyja were said to be hostages. Some believe that events that occurred between the Æsir and Vanir were a reflection of events common between different Norse clans at the time. The Æsir did not grow old and instead remaining young by eating the apples of Iðunn. While they did not age, they could be killed. It was said that most of them woulld die at Ragnarök. Baldr - God of light and radiance, he is the most beloved of the gods. He is the son of Odin and Frigg and younger brother of Thor. Frigg - Wife of Odin and goddess of marriage, she rules Asgard as queen alongside the All-Father. Heimdallr - Known as the All-Seeing, he is the guardian of the rainbow bridge Bifröst. Höðr - God of winter and darkness; a blind god, he is the son of Odin and Frigg. Iðunn - Goddess of youth, she was keeper of the apples that grant the gods their phenomenal longevity and youth. Loki - Though oftentimes referred to as the god of trickery and mischief, Loki is not counted among the Æsir. The son of the jötunn Laufey and Fárbauti (Old Norse: “cruel striker”), he is Odin’s blood brother. Odin - God of wisdom, poetry and war, he is chief of the Æsir and ruler of Asgard. Sif - Goddess of agriculture and fertility, she is the beloved wife of Thor, known across the Nine Worlds for her golden hair, which was sheared by Loki. Thor - God of thunder and lightning, he is Asgard's greatest champion. He is the eldest son of Odin, born to him by Jörð, the personification of the Earth. Týr - God of law and heroic glory, he is one-handed. Either the son of Odin or the jotunn Hymir and Hroðr (Old Norse: “famed”). Ullr - God of the hunt and archery, he is the son of Sif and Thor's stepson. Viðarr - God of vengeance, he is the son of Odin and the female jötunn Gríðr.

In Norse mythology, Aegir is the god of the seas. He is the king of all the oceans. Aegir was feared by sailors, for this god would sink ships and take cargo. Aegir was worshiped by sailors who were afraid of him and sailors who were not. He has a wife named Ran and with her, they had nine daughters called the "waves". They had a son with Odin, Heimdall.

Île Saint-Louis is connected to the rest of Paris by four bridges to both banks of the river and to the Île de la Cité by the Pont Saint-Louis. The island was first known as the Île Notre-Dame and was used mostly for grazing cattle, fishing, drying laundry, and occasionally for fighting duels. It was originally owned by the chapter of Notre-Dame cathedral.

In Norse mythology, Óðr (sometimes written in English as Odr or Od) is a man associated with the goddess Freyja. The Prose Edda and Heimskringla, both by Snorri Sturluson, describe Óðr as Freyja's husband. They also describe him as the father of Freyja's daughter Hnoss. Heimskringla adds that the couple had another daughter together, Gersemi. Not much else is written about Óðr, except that he often went away on long journeys. Freyja wept when she missed him. Several scholars have suggested that Óðr may just have been another name for the god Odin.When Freyja wept, she wept tears of red gold, which was very valuable and precious, and this is what she used to give to heroes to do jobs for her so that they had something to bargain with.

Öggestorp Church is a church building in Öggestorp, Sweden. It belongs to the Rogberga-Öggestorp Parish of the Church of Sweden. The church was opened on 18 August 1883. It replaced replacing the old church. The older church was demolished in 1882.
The Örgryte New Church is a church building in Örgryte in the town of Gothenburg in Sweden. It belongs to the Örgryte Parish of the Church of Sweden. The church was opened on 6 July 1890.

The Örgryte Old Church is a church building in Örgryte in the town of Gothenburg in Sweden. It belongs to the Örgryte Parish of the Church of Sweden. A church at the present site of the Örgryte Old Church has been around since the 13th century.

The Örebro Mission was a Protestant denomination in Sweden. It was founded in the town of Örebro in 1892 It was part of the Baptist Union of Sweden until 1936. In 1997 the denomination became part of the Evangelical Free Church in Sweden.
Österängen Church is a church building at Österängen in Jönköping in Sweden. It belongs to the Christina-Ljungarum Parish of the Church of Sweden. It was inaugurated on First Advent Sunday 1961.

The Östra Torp Church is a church building in Smygehamn in Sweden. I belongs to the Källtorp Parish of the Church of Sweden. It was inaugurated on 14 June 1911. It replaced an older church which had been destroyed by a fire in 1909. The church is the southernmost in Sweden.

Öxnehaga Church is a church building at Öxnehaga in Huskvarna in Sweden. It belongs to the Huskvarna Parish of the Church of Sweden. It was inaugurated on 27 November 1976. That date was the Saturday before the First Advent Sunday that year.

Ēostre is a goddess of Spring in Germanic paganism. The festival of Easter is named after her. Her colors are pink and green. Eostre is a symbol of rebirth and fertility. Her animal is the hare - which is the origin of the Easter Bunny.

Ōmononushi is a god in Japanese mythology who is connected to Mount Miwa in Sakurai, Nara Prefecture. He is closely related to the god Ōkuninushi in the imperial myth cycle, with the Nihon Shoki and Kojiki texts referring to Ōmononushi as either another name or a spirit of Ōkuninushi. Ōmononushi is mainly worshipped at Ōmiwa Shrine located at the base of Mount Miwa. This mountain is considered the shrine's sacred object of worship. Ōmononushi is also known as Miwa-no-Ōkami or Miwa (Dai)myōjin. He is also worshipped at Ōsugi Shrine in Ibaraki Prefecture, and is identified with Konpira Daigongen, the deity of Kotohira Shrine in Kagawa Prefecture.

Ōmonoimi-no-Kami is a Japanese god who is said to reside on Mount Chōkai in Yamagata Prefecture, in Japan. There are shrines that enshrine Ōmonoimi-no-Kami in various places in the Tohoku region, including Chokaisan Ōmonoimi Shrine, on the summit of Mount Chōkai, and Chōkai gassan ryōsho-gu. The goddess is considered to be possibly identical to Toyōke Ōmikami, Mount Chōkai is in the northern area of Yamato sovereignty. Its people believed that Daimotsui no kami protected their nation and purified kegare. The mountain is a volcano, and there have been eruptions in the past. Ōmonoimi-no-Kami is considered to be the same deity as Uka no mitama, Toyouke no Okami, Oimimi no kami, or Hirose no kami. According to the shrine tradition of Chōkaisan Ōmonoimi Shrine, it is the same deity as Toyōke Ōmikami of. Chōkai Gassan Ryōsho-gu enshrines Kurinama no Mikoto as the deity of Mount Chōkai. According to legend, a three-legged crow, a sacred crow, was sent to observe the evil deeds of a being with long arms. The raven would make a sound of "Yes" to signal the appearance of the being and "Muya" when it did not appear. 2=大国主 is a god in Japanese stories. People who practice the Shinto religion worship him. Ōkuninushi is one of the most important Shinto gods, along with Amaterasu and Susanoo. He is more important in Izumo Shinto than Ise Shinto. He is an important figure in Kojiki and Nihon Shoki, two old books about myths. Some stories say Susanoo is Ōkuninushi's ancestor and others say he is his father. In the stories, Ōkuninushi is in charge of the gods who protect the earth. He used to be the ruler of a place called Ashihara no Nakatsukuni. But when the gods in the sky asked him to give up his power, Ōkuninushi agreed and went to a hidden world. He was given that world to rule. Later, Amaterasu's grandson, Ninigi, came to Ashihara no Nakatsukuni to rule it. Ninigi became the first Japanese emperor's ancestor. Ōkuninushi is associated with the province of Izumo. This region may have been taken over by the Yamato court, and his surrender to the gods of heaven in myth might reflect this. The Fudoki, a gazetteer report of Izumo province from the early 7th century, contains many myths about Ōkuninushi and related deities. He is also featured in the Fudoki of other provinces like Harima. Ōkuninushi is known for having many romantic affairs with goddesses, resulting in the birth of many divine offspring, including the gods Kotoshironushi and Takeminakata. Ōkuninushi is worshiped in many Shinto shrines across Japan, but the most famous one is the Grand Shrine of Izumo in Shimane. The Izumo Taishakyō group, which is based in this shrine, considers him their central deity. Ōkuninushi was also combined with the Buddhist deity Daikokuten before the Meiji period, when Buddhism and Shinto were blended.
Ōmiya-no-Me is a Japanese goddess. She is worshipped in the Hasshinden. She is sometimes identified with Ame-no-Uzume. At Fushimi Inari-taisha she is one of the three parts of Inari Ōkami.
